Learning Objectives
Understand the etiology, differential diagnosis, and risk factors of metatarsalgia.
Perform an appropriate workup of patients with suspected metatarsalgia.
Specify the operative and nonoperative management of metatarsalgia.
Pathophysiology and Pathoanatomy
Overview
Metatarsalgia is defined as pain across the plantar forefoot beneath the second, third, and
fourth metatarsal heads.1 (Resource 1).
Symptoms may be related to increased pressure or decreased padding under the affected
metatarsal heads.

Associated interdigital neuritis or metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint instability, synovitis, or
arthritis may be present.
Management involves directly or indirectly off-loading the affected metatarsal, which may
include addressing associated deformities, muscle imbalance, or ligament instability.
Anatomy
Osteology
The metatarsals articulate proximally with the cuneiforms and the cuboid and distally with the
proximal phalanges.
Joints and Ligaments
The MTP joint is stabilized by the capsule, the plantar plate, and the medial and lateral
collateral ligaments (Figure 1).
The deep transverse metatarsal ligaments connect the second through fifth distal metatarsals,
but not the first, inserting instead on the lateral sesamoid (Figure 2).

collateral ligaments (accessory collateral ligament [ACL] and proper collateral ligament [PCL])

A fat pad under the metatarsal head provides cushioning with weight bearing. The fat pad has
attachments to the proximal phalangeal base and may move distal to the metatarsal head with
extensive dorsiflexion of the MTP joint.
Tendons
Dorsiflexion of the lesser MTP joints is provided by the extensor digitorum longus and the
extensor digitorum brevis for the second through fourth toes.
Plantar flexion of the lesser MTP joints is principally provided by the seven interossei (four
dorsal and three plantar) and four lumbricals, the tendons of which travel dorsal and plantar,
respectively, to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.
Plantar flexion of the lesser MTP joints also is provided by the flexor digitorum longus and
the flexor digitorum brevis for the second through fourth toes, but their primary effect is on
the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints.
Dorsal dislocation of the MTP joint or plantar displacement of the metatarsal head after
osteotomy may result in the interossei tendons moving dorsally relative to the MTP joint axis,
making them less effective MTP plantar flexors or potential dorsiflexors of the joint.
Nerves

The interdigital nerves run plantar to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament the location at
which they may be compressed, leading to interdigital neuritis or Morton neuroma.
The plantar forefoot is innervated by branches of the tibial nerve, with the medial plantar
nerve providing sensation to the medial three and one-half toes and the lateral plantar nerve
providing sensation to the lateral one and one-half toes.
Biomechanics
Increased length and/or plantar angulation of a metatarsal relative to the other four
metatarsals or a prominent plantar condyle may increase weight-bearing forces under the
metatarsal head.
Achilles tendon or isolated gastrocnemius contractures transfer weight-bearing forces from
the heel to the forefoot.

Biomechanics
Hypermobility of the first tarsometatarsal joint, often observed in patients with
moderate to severe hallux valgus deformity, may transfer weight-bearing force from the
first metatarsal head and the sesamoids to the lesser metatarsal heads, particularly the
second.
Midfoot cavus may increase forefoot weight bearing, and hindfoot varus and valgus may
increase lateral and medial forefoot weight bearing.
These triceps surae contractures also may result in extensor recruitment of the extensor
digitorum longus to assist the anterior tibialis in dorsiflexion of the ankle, leading to
increased dorsiflexion at the lesser MTP joints and distal migration of the plantar fat pad
from under the lesser metatarsal heads.
Etiology
Predisposing anatomic factors include an elongated second or third metatarsal relative to the
first metatarsal, a prominent plantar condyle of the metatarsal head (Figure 3), triceps surae
contracture, cavus foot, hallux valgus, hammer or claw toe deformity, and brachymetatarsia.

Shoes with high heels; narrow toe boxes; and flexible, minimally cushioned soles may increase
weight-bearing forces under the metatarsal heads.
Inflammatory arthritis may lead to synovitis and ligament instability.
MTP corticosteroid injections may lead to ligament attenuation and instability.
Trauma or forefoot surgery may lead to plantar metatarsal malunion with increased weight
bearing or dorsal malunion with transfer metatarsalgia.
Figure 3: Schematic cross section shows a prominent plantar condyle that has resulted in an
intractable plantar keratosis. (Reproduced from Kakadia AR: Metatarsalgia, in Chou LB, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 213-224.)
Classification
Although no universally agreed on classification system exists for metatarsalgia, the causes
have been subjectively subdivided into three groups: primary, secondary, and iatrogenic1,2
(Table 1).
Primary metatarsalgia results from the anatomic characteristics of the affected metatarsal(s)
relative to the other bones in the foot.
Secondary metatarsalgia results from indirect mechanisms that transfer stress to the
affected metatarsal(s).

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients report pain under the affected metatarsal head(s).
The pain typically is worse while walking barefoot.
Conversely, patients with Morton neuroma often report pain relief on removing shoe wear.
The patient may note progression or new development of a hammer toe or varus/valgus toe
deformity.
Physical Examination
Tenderness is present under the affected metatarsal head(s).
A callus or intractable plantar keratosis may be present under the affected metatarsal head(s).
The metatarsal head may be prominent plantarly, and the fat pad under it may be thin or
displaced distally.
With associated MTP synovitis or arthritis, MTP swelling with decreased, painful range of
motion may be present.
With an associated plantar plate tear, tenderness over the plantar proximal phalangeal base, a
painful and/or positive drawer sign, and clawing/ hammering and/or asymmetric splaying of
the toe may be present.
The drawer test, also referred to as the Lachman test, is performed by stabilizing the
metatarsal head between the thumb and index finger of one hand and applying dorsal stress
to the proximal phalangeal base with the thumb and index finger of the other hand (Figure
4).

Figure 4: Illustrations show the drawer test, which can be used to detect
metatarsophalangeal joint instability. The joint is held in a neutral position (A), and vertical
force is then applied in a dorsal direction (B). (Reproduced from Doty JF, Coughlin MJ:
Metatarsophalangeal joint instability of the lesser toes and plantar plate deficiency. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2014;22[4]:235-245.)
In patients with severe metatarsalgia, a crossover toe deformity may develop secondary to
plantar plate and collateral ligament insufficiency, with the toe becoming clawed and crossing
over the adjacent medial or lateral toe, most commonly the second toe over the hallux.
Dorsal MTP tenderness is more common in patients with Freiberg infraction and arthritis.
With associated hammer toes, the MTP joint may be dorsiflexed, dorsally subluxed, or
dislocated.
The adjacent interdigital web space may be tender from associated synovitis compressing the
interdigital nerve against the adjacent metatarsals and the transverse metatarsal ligament
and/or MTP dorsiflexion tenting the interdigital nerve against the ligament. A concurrent
Morton neuroma may develop in patients with long-standing interdigital nerve compression
and physical damage to the nerve.
The pain may be increased by squeezing the metatarsal heads together, dorsiflexing the
adjacent toes, or attempting to elicit a Mulder click by dorsally and plantarly translating the
adjacent metatarsal heads relative to each other.
Neurovascular Examination
Plantar foot sensation should be assessed, including with the use of a Semmes-Weinstein 5.07
monofilament, because neuropathy may result in plantar forefoot pain. Tenderness or a Tinel
sign may be present over the tarsal tunnel or the proximal abductor hallucis because of
compression of the tibial nerve or its branches. The interdigital nerve may be tender in the

adjacent toes.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs should be obtained and assessed for
overall foot deformity; relative metatarsal length; fracture; and MTP joint arthritis, angular
deformity, and subluxation/ dislocation. A metatarsal head view, which is an axial sesamoid
view of the entire forefoot, also should be obtained because it may demonstrate sesamoid
pathology and the relative plantar prominence of the lesser metatarsal heads (Figure 5).

appears longer than the first and third metatarsals. On the lateral view (B), the outline of first,
second, and third metatarsal heads is difficult to clearly visualize because of overlap. On the
metatarsal head view (C), the second metatarsal is at approximately the same level as the
sesamoids and is dorsal to the third metatarsal head. Therefore, an isolated shortening or
dorsiflexion osteotomy of the second metatarsal would be associated with a high risk of

transfer metatarsalgia of the third metatarsal head. (Courtesy of Michael S. Aronow, MD,
FAAOS, Hartford, CT.)
Hindfoot varus and valgus can be assessed via a weight-bearing Cobey/Saltzman hindfoot
alignment view. A weight-bearing AP knee radiograph can be obtained in patients with genu
valgum or varum.
Computed Tomography
CT scans, particularly weight-bearing CT scans, may show metatarsal head position and MTP
joint subluxation, as well as other associated pathology, including occult fracture and arthritis.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be used to assess for the presence and extent of associated pathology, including
fracture, bursitis, arthritis/synovitis, Morton neuroma, Freiberg infraction, and plantar plate
disruption.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can be used to assess for associated pathology, including Morton neuroma
and plantar plate tears.
Other Imaging Studies
MTP arthrography can be used to show plantar plate tears.
Diagnosis
Metatarsalgia can be diagnosed if pain is present beneath the second, third, and/or fourth
metatarsal heads. The cause(s) of the metatarsalgia are diagnosed via the patient history;
physical examination findings; imaging study findings; and response to diagnostic/potential
therapeutic treatment options, such as anesthetic-containing injections.
Differential Diagnosis

Any disorder that results in pain under the central metatarsal heads may be considered a
cause or an associated condition of metatarsalgia. MTP synovitis, MTP instability, interdigital
neuritis, Morton neuroma, plantar warts, occult fracture, stress reaction, and Freiberg
infraction may result in metatarsalgia (Table 1).
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management includes rest; activity modifications; shoe modifications; orthoses to
off-load the affected metatarsal head; splints to correct MTP hyperextension associated with
claw toe deformities; analgesic and anti-inflammatory medications, including NSAIDs; callus
paring; immobilization of an unstable or synovitic MTP joint; and toe strengthening exercises.
Steroid injections should be used with caution because they may result in additional soft-
tissue attenuation that may lead to MTP instability.
Stabilization of the MTP joint in neutral dorsiflexion via taping or with the use of a Budin toe
splint relocates the plantar fat pad under the metatarsal head, allows an inflamed MTP joint to
rest, and decreases stress on a plantar plate tear (Figure 6). The restricted motion is
reinforced with the use of an accommodative shoe with a stiff forefoot rocker and a cushioned
insole.
Figure 6: Photographs of feet show metatarsophalangeal joint stabilization. Plantar (A) and
dorsal (B) view photographs show a toe taped in a reduced position. C, Photograph shows the
use of a Budin splint, which may be better tolerated than toe taping. (Reproduced from Doty
JF, Coughlin MJ: Metatarsophalangeal joint instability of the lesser toes and plantar plate
deficiency. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[4]:235-245.)

Orthotics
Initial off-loading is achieved via the use of appropriate shoe wear and off-the-shelf or over-
the-counter insoles and/or metatarsal pads (Figure 7).
Figure 7: Photograph shows a cushioned insole with a metatarsal bar pad over a carbon
fiber plate. (Reproduced from Doty JF, Coughlin MJ: Shoes and orthoses, in Chou LB, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 13-23.)
Occasionally, an additional layer of gel or other cushioned material in combination with a
thin-soled shoe is sufficient.

Nonsurgical Management
Low-heel, accommodative shoes with a stiff forefoot rocker and a cushioned insole also
limit MTP motion and decrease weight-bearing stress. Flexible shoes may be made more
rigid by inserting a turf toe plate or a carbon fiber insole under a removable cushioned
insole.
Removing a hard callus with the use of a knife or a pumice stone may afford transient
pain relief, particularly if a deep seed corn is present. The presence of black dots under
the callus suggests a plantar wart.
Gastrocnemius stretching exercises may shift weight-bearing stress from the metatarsal
heads to the heel.
A 2-month home toe exercise program may improve toe grip strength and decrease pain
in patients
with metatarsalgia.5

If these methods are not sufficient, a transferable material, such as lipstick, can be
placed under the symptomatic plantar metatarsal head(s), and the patient then steps on
the orthotic, leaving a mark on it. The marked area on the orthotic can be cut out,
allowing the affected metatarsal head(s) to float over the depression, or a metatarsal
pad can be placed proximal to it, with the pad often tolerated better on the
undersurface of the insole.
If these methods are not helpful, a more expensive custom orthosis generated from a
mold or weight-bearing measurements of the patient’s foot can be fabricated.
One option contains a semirigid base with a soft, full-length cover with a depression
under or a metatarsal bar proximal the affected metatarsal head(s).In patients with
neuropathy or lower demands, a plastazote orthotic will mold with weight bearing to
distribute weight more evenly across the forefoot.
Indications 

Indications
Nonsurgical management often is successful in resolving the cause or managing the
symptoms of metatarsalgia With a few exceptions, nonsurgical management should be
attempted for at least 3 to 6 months before considering surgical management.
Contraindications
In patients with clinically important infection, surgical excision of metatarsal head
osteomyelitis or débridement of submetatarsal head ulcers with off-loading via triceps surae
lengthening or condylectomy may be required acutely.
Surgical Management
Indications

Surgical treatment is indicated in symptomatic patients who are not responsive to appropriate
nonsurgical management.
Surgical treatment may be considered acutely in patients with ulceration and infection and
patients with a fixed deformity in whom nonsurgical treatment fails and additional treatment
options are unlikely to be successful or tolerated as a long-term option.
Contraindications
Potential surgical contraindications include clinically important medical comorbidities, poor
vascular status, and likely noncompliance with postoperative management.
Techniques and Procedures
Metatarsalgia can be managed surgically via off-loading the affected metatarsal head. This off-
loading can be achieved directly by shortening the metatarsal or dorsally translating the
affected metatarsal head via a metatarsal osteotomy or tarsometatarsal arthrodesis or,
alternatively, by removing bone and cartilage from the distal or plantar aspect of the
metatarsal head.
These procedures can be performed via open or minimally invasive techniques, with the
latter associated with the advantages of smaller incisions and less soft-tissue dissection,
which may be particularly helpful in high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes mellitus
but also associated with disadvantages, including complications associated with a high
learning curve for the procedure.
Metatarsal osteotomies can be performed in the distal, diaphyseal, or proximal
metatarsal.6,7
Condylectomy is indicated if a prominent condyle is associated with an intractable plantar
keratosis8 and may be considered in patients with a plantar ulcer or if the surgeon wants to
avoid the potential increased morbidity or recovery time associated with a metatarsal
osteotomy.
Correcting the MTP hyperextension deformity of an associated claw or hammer toe deformity
may relocate the distally migrated fat pad back under the affected lesser metatarsal head,
thereby providing cushioning and decreasing biomechanical stress.
Metatarsal head off-loading can be accomplished indirectly by transferring weight-bearing load
to other parts of the foot.

Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession transfers load from the affected
metatarsal to the heel.
Correction of a hallux valgus deformity with a hypermobile first ray transfers weight from the
affected metatarsal to the first metatarsal and sesamoids.
Metatarsal head excision may be performed in patients with substantial osteomyelitis but may
lead to transfer metatarsalgia.
Excision of multiple lesser metatarsal heads may be appropriate, with substantial
inflammatory arthritis affecting multiple MTP joints or with lesser MTP dislocations and
patient morbidity making multiple metatarsal osteotomies less desirable.9
Intra-articular pathology may be addressed via MTP joint débridement and synovectomy,
exostectomy, and microfracture; osteochondral grafts; or intra-articular dorsiflexion
osteotomies for osteochondral lesions in patients with disorders such as Freiberg infraction.
Associated pathology that is not responsive to nonsurgical management and may be
contributing to metatarsalgia symptoms, including hammer toes, plantar plate tears, and
Morton neuroma, may be addressed.
Plantar plate repair or advancement may be performed with or without metatarsal
osteotomy.

Techniques and Procedures
Correction of hindfoot varus via a calcaneal osteotomy or hindfoot arthrodesis transfers
load from an affected fourth or fifth metatarsal.
Dorsiflexion osteotomies and/or arthrodeses of the midfoot and/or a Steindler stripping
of the calcaneal origin of the plantar fascia and plantar foot intrinsic muscles can be
performed for the management of metatarsalgia secondary to a cavus foot.
In patients with advanced MTP arthritis, interposition arthroplasty is an alternative to
decrease the risk of transfer metatarsalgia.10
Dorsal and plantar approaches can be used, with dorsal visualization aided by MTP joint
distraction or arthroscopy.11,12 The flexor digitorum longus or its sheath can be used to
augment the plantar plate directly via a plantar approach13 or indirectly via a
Girdlestone-Taylor procedure, which may be performed via the standard dorsal and
plantar approach or, alternatively, via the medial or lateral aspect of the proximal
phalanx, depending on whether any associated MTP varus or valgus deformity is

present.14,15
Morton neuroma or interdigital neuritis occasionally responds to indirect decompression
of the interdigital nerve secondary to metatarsal osteotomy, metatarsal exostectomy, or
decreased MTP synovitis.
If no substantial internal damage to the interdigital nerve is present, it may respond to
surgical decompression via transverse metatarsal ligament release, which typically is
performed via a dorsal open or endoscopic approach, with or without concurrent
metatarsal osteotomy.16,17
A large neuroma or a damaged nerve may be resected via a dorsal or plantar approach,
and the proximal nerve stump may be allowed to retract proximal to the metatarsal
heads or may be directly buried into interosseus muscle.18,19
Hammer or claw toe deformities can be addressed via open or percutaneous flexor
digitorum longus and/or flexor digitorum brevis tenotomies, Girdlestone-Taylor flexor-
to-extensor tendon transfer, proximal phalangeal joint arthrodesis or resection

Associated MTP extension contractions may be addressed via dorsal MTP capsulotomy
with or without partial collateral ligament and plantar plate release with the use of a

Transverse plane MTP angular deformities may require medial or lateral collateral
ligament release, with imbrication of the other collateral ligament or tendon transfer,
such as the extensor digitorum brevis.
Triceps surae contracture not responsive to stretching exercises may be managed via
percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession, depending on
the location of the contracture and the patient’s morbidity.20,21

procedures are determined based on the patient’s symptoms, pathology, and goals, as well as
the surgeon’s skills.
If a metatarsal osteotomy is planned, the amount of shortening and dorsal translation
required is estimated.

Surgical Approaches
For a dorsal approach, the incision typically is centered over the affected metatarsal head or
the adjacent intermetatarsal space. Protecting the dorsal sensory nerves, the MTP capsule and
the extensor tendons are exposed. If planned, an extensor tenotomy or Z-lengthening is
performed. If not, the dorsal periosteum and capsule are exposed by retracting the extensor
digitorum longus and brevis tendons laterally or medially and elevating the interossei muscles
as necessary to provide bone exposure. The metatarsal head can be exposed via a transverse
capsulotomy, subperiosteal release of the collateral ligaments from the metatarsal head, and
partial freeing of the plantar plate with the use of a McGlamry elevator.
For a plantar approach, the incision typically is made medial or lateral to the weight-bearing
portion of the metatarsal head.
Condylectomy typically is performed via a dorsal approach, with a McGlamry elevator used to
aid in exposure of the plantar condyle(s).
The plantar condyles also can be exposed through a plantar ulcer. The cut typically is made
parallel to the plantar metatarsal diaphyseal cortex (Figure 8, Resource 2).

Surgical Approaches
If an ulcer is present under the metatarsal head, it may be excised and directly closed;
closed via a rotational flap or allowed to heal secondarily with dressing changes, skin
substitutes or skin grafts; or closed via vacuum-assisted closure, with any metatarsal
head plantar prominence or osteomyelitis addressed via the plantar ulcer or a
separate dorsal incision. Taking care to protect interdigital nerves and intrinsic
tendons, the flexor tendon sheath is opened, the flexor digitorum longus and flexor
digitorum brevis tendons are retracted, and the plantar plate is exposed.
Fixation typically is achieved with the use of a lag screw or a dorsal plate. Ideally, the
plantar cortex is left intact as a hinge, and the amount of dorsal bone removed

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management protocols depend on the procedure performed, the quality of
fixation achieved, the approach used, and surgeon preference.
Patients typically use a weight-bearing orthopaedic shoe, avoiding the toe-off position, unless
concern exists with regard to metatarsal osteotomy fixation strength or patient compliance,
situations in which a short leg cast with a toeplate may be used.
Plantar incisions typically are off-loaded for at least 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively until healed.

Complications
The most common surgical complications, include infection, wound dehiscence, nerve injury,
tendon injury, recurrence, complex regional pain syndrome, and anesthetic complications, and
may occur after any surgical procedure for the management of metatarsalgia.
Metatarsal osteotomies also may be associated with malunion, nonunion, transfer
metatarsalgia, symptomatic hardware, osteonecrosis, and MTP stiffness.
Floating toes can occur after any metatarsal osteotomy but are more commonly associated
with the Weil osteotomy.
Vascular compromise of the toes, occasionally substantial enough to result in gangrene or
amputation, may result from damage to the medial and lateral interdigital arteries to the toe
secondary to dissection on both sides of the metatarsal or result from tension because of
correction of a chronically dislocated hammer toe.

Complications
Floating toes rest without making contact with the ground and often are associated with
decreased MTP plantar flexion strength. Floating toes may result from dorsal soft-tissue
contracture related to surgical exposure; lack of postoperative MTP splinting or plantar
flexion exercises; or decreased MTP plantar flexion strength secondary to excessive
plantar or proximal translation of the metatarsal head, leading to dorsal translation of
the dorsal interossei tendons relative to the axis of the MTP joint and decreased tendon
tension.24,31
Care should be taken during the excision of Morton neuromas from adjacent web
spaces, given the proximity of the interdigital nerve and vessels. Removal of the more
symptomatic one and decompression of the other is not unreasonable.
The tourniquet should be released after pinning of an MTP joint. If the toe remains pale
after observation and the application of warm, saline-soaked gauze, then the surgeon
should consider backing out the K-wire to the proximal phalangeal base.
